# ADR-0023 first batch — the stop-and-look

*Measured 2026-10-26. The batch is generated by `engine.denominator.first_batch`, not chosen —
stratified by `source_type`, proportional to the 65-source read corpus, alphabetical within each
stratum. Re-runnable.*

## The result

**`stated` holds 12 of 15, which is 80.0%.** The threshold ADR-0023 section 3 fixed in advance is
**more than 85%**, so **the failure condition does not fire and the ADR survives its own test.**

It survives by three percentage points. One source classified the other way takes it to 86.7% and
retires it. That margin is the reason the number was fixed before the batch was read.

## ⚠️ These are not audit-standard reads, and must not be recorded as if they were

The audit's other four properties carry `basis: verified_against_artifact`, which means somebody
opened the document and read it. **What produced the table above is targeted text search over
extracted text** — `pdftotext` and stripped HTML, grepped for base-naming language and sample
sizes. It is strong enough to answer the question section 3 asks (*does this property
discriminate between sources?*) and **not** strong enough to write into `sources/audit.yaml`.

Recording these as verified would be the exact false precision ADR-0023 section 2 forbids, in the
ADR that forbids it. So nothing has been written to the audit file. The batch answers the
stop-and-look and stops.

What was actually seen, per source, is below — that part is quoted and real.

## What the evidence was

**`stated`, with the base named in the document's own words**

- **Cyentia IRIS 2022** — the strongest in the batch, and it states the limit as well as the base.
  *"78% of impacted firms experienced a single event between 2012-2021"*, and in a footnote to the
  frequency model: *"Since we don't have a reliable count of all active firms around the world, we
  can't say how many had zero incidents. Only firms with at least one publicly known cyber event
  are in our dataset."* A publisher naming the denominator it does not have.
- **IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2025** — chart bases are labelled, not inferred.
  *"Among the organizations that had fully recovered"*, *"From organizations that reported fully
  recovering from a data breach"*, *"Among those organizations that experienced fines"*.
- **Verizon DBIR 2025** — `n=` on the figures themselves, e.g. *"Figure 5. Known initial access
  vectors in non-Error, non-Misuse breaches (n=9,891)"*. Note the base is **breaches**, not
  organizations, which is the single most mistranslated base in this corpus.
- **ESAs DORA major incidents 2025** — *"Share of major incidents…"* throughout, and the rate is
  put against a named denominator: *"When compared to the total number of FEs subject to DORA."*
- **Gurucul Insider Risk 2026** — *"With 725 respondents, this survey carries a margin of error of
  approximately +/- 3.6 percentage points at a 95% confidence level."*
- **Bitkom Wirtschaftsschutz 2025** — 26 explicit `Basis:` labels, `n=1.002` and `n=868`. German
  survey convention puts the base under the chart.
- **Cybersecurity Insiders Insider Threat 2024** — *"survey of 413"*, bases given as respondents.
- **Interos 2022** — `n=1,500` on eleven figures, *"surveyed 1,500"*.
- **ASD Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024-25** — *"of all incidents"* against a stated report count.
- **ABS, both releases** — official statistics; *"of all businesses"*, *"proportion of
  businesses"*. These are denominator sources in their own right, which is why two shards use them
  as one.
- **BCI Supply Chain Resilience 2024** — *weakest of the twelve.* It names the base — *"17.1% of
  respondents"*, *"20% of respondents"* — but never states how many respondents there are. The
  base is named and unquantified. Flagged because if `stated` is read strictly as *named and
  countable*, this one moves, and the batch goes to 11 of 15.

**`not_applicable` — the source publishes no percentage**

- **AFP BEC victim case 2021** and **Arup deepfake case 2024.** Single-incident reports, zero
  percentage expressions in either. There is no base to name, which is an honest answer rather
  than a gap.

**`ambiguous`**

- **Deepfake business impact 2024.** A compilation article that borrows its percentages from third
  parties and fixes the base for none of them — *"According to a McAfee survey, 70 percent of
  people…"*, *"more than 95 percent of deepfake videos are created with its open-source
  software"* (the claim is the software vendor's own). The document prints percentages whose base
  it does not itself establish.

## What this says, before anyone decides what to do about it

**The direction is strong even though the threshold held.** Twelve of fifteen publishers state
what their percentages are over, and several do it carefully — Cyentia names a denominator it
cannot obtain, Verizon puts the count on the figure, Bitkom labels every chart.

So the defect is **not** that publishers hide their bases. It is that the base lives in a chart
label, a footnote or a methodology page, and the sentence that gets quoted does not carry it. That
is the finding the 2026-10-24 post was already written around, and this batch is the first
measured support for it rather than an impression.

**What it costs the ADR.** A column that reads `stated` 80% of the time is close to ceremony, and
section 3 was written because that is a real failure. It cleared, but a remedy whose value is
concentrated in roughly a fifth of the corpus should be sized accordingly — the 50 remaining
re-reads buy less than the first framing assumed.

## The screen, and what it is worth — measured 2026-10-26

ADR-0023's amendment drops the corpus-wide re-read, which turns the work into a screening problem.
`engine.denominator.screen` nominates sources by reading **our own audit prose** rather than the
artifact, on the reasoning that those four answers are already a verified reading by someone who
opened the document.

Validated against the only ground truth available, these 15:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| nominated, and worth reading | 3 |
| nominated, but already `stated` | 7 |
| settled, and already `stated` | 5 |
| settled, but worth reading | **0** |
| **precision** | **30%** |
| **recall** | 100%, on 15 sources |

**Read that as a conservative filter, not a precise one.** It cuts 65 sources to 38 with no
observed miss, which is worth having. It also means roughly two of every three nominated reads will
confirm what the record already implied. The recall figure rests on fifteen sources and should be
read as *no miss was observed*, not as *there are none*.

**The false positives show why no prose screen can do much better.** `cyentia_iris_2022` is
nominated and is the strongest `stated` in the batch — it names a denominator it cannot obtain. Our
four answers never quoted that part because they were written to answer four other questions. A
screen over our prose can only measure what our prose happened to mention.

## Open, and owed to the owner

1. **Is `stated` *named* or *named and countable*?** BCI turns on it, and so will others. Deciding
   it after seeing which way it moves the threshold is the move ADR-0017 exists to warn about, so
   it should be decided on the definition and not on the count.
2. **Do the 15 get full audit-standard reads before anything is written?** Nothing is in
   `sources/audit.yaml` yet and nothing should be until they do.
3. **Is the remaining 50 worth it**, given the direction? An honest alternative is to record the
   finding, keep the field for sources where the base is genuinely unclear, and not re-read the
   whole corpus to write `stated` fifty more times.
